newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair promises Britain a fresh start.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair promises Britain a fresh start.

text.p: Opposition leader Tony Blair, launching the Labour Party's manifesto for a May 1 election, on Thursday made 10 promises in a "contract with the people" to govern Britain from the political centre ground.

A day after the ruling Conservatives launched their policy blueprint, Blair promised not to raise income tax rates, to guarantee low inflation, to get thousands of young people back to work and to show leadership in Europe.
"I defy anyone to deny this is a radical programme. But it is in the radical centre, modern, forward-looking and utterly in tune with the times and instincts of today's Britain," Blair said.

"It is, in other words, New Labour, neither a programme of the left nor the Conservatives. It breaks new ground and seeks to build genuine support in all parts of the nation behind it. That is what we offer to Britain today. A fresh start. A new beginning. Not before time."

Blair told a news conference that with the publication of the programmes of the two main parties, voters now had a real choice "between the future and the past, between a party for the many and a party for the few, between leadership and drift".
Blair said voters would be able to judge Labour, which has been out of power for 18 years, on whether they fulfilled the 10 pledges.

"We make a virtue of the fact that our manifesto does not promise the earth. It does not say it can do everything. There are no magic wands or instant solutions. What we do say is: Britain deserves better,'" he said.

Labour is widely tipped to win the election and leads the Conservatives in opinion polls. The latest opinion poll in The Times newspaper put Labour at 55 percent, far ahead of the Conservatives who trailed at 28 percent.

In the manifesto Blair says education will be his government's "Number One priority", and spending on it will rise. He also vows to use a windfall tax on surplus profits of water, gas, electricity and other firms privatised by the Conservatives to take 250,000 people our of the dole queues.

Other pledges included in Labour's contract with the people include more money for National Health Service patient care, the safeguarding of Britain's environment, a cleanup of politics following a bout of sleaze and to "give Britain the leadership in Europe which Britain and Europe need."

Blair, who will be the the youngest prime minister this century if he is elected, also pledged to remove what he called the two-tier health system, to cut waiting lists and improve treatment for breast cancer.
On the issue of a European single currency he confirmed the issue would be put to the British public in a referendum but the government would keep its options open.
